question: Sheel Shah, JP Morgan. First, in the US cards, coming back to the NIM. Can I ask if you think that greater than 12% is still achievable for 2026, given you're holding maybe a bit more excess liquidity from deposits, revolver balances are maybe a little lower than you'd expect? Secondly, on the markets VAR, the £23 million in the first quarter, that's a lot lower than your 2024 average of around £26 million, or even lower than your 2023 average. What are you doing behind the scenes here? I know that inventory risk is lower, using capital more efficiently, but any tangible examples you can give around this?
answer: Let me start with US cards, yes, we believe it's [still] achievable. What you're seeing in Q1 is a slightly odd picture, impacted by a couple of things. The first is, as Fed rates reduce in any particular quarter, you're going to see some degree of compression in NIM, but then offset in non-interest income. We've got floating rate assets, largely fixed rate liabilities that take time to reprice. We do hedge the position, but it's not the kind of structural hedging that you see within BUK, and the income from that hedge actually flows into non-NII. So it's a little bit messy, but you can see year-on-year that non-NII is much stronger, and that's really the effect of that hedge. But on an underlying basis, no real pressure on income. The other thing that's going on in Q1 is, what I would describe as a full NIM, it's not a banking NIM. So we have some cash sitting on the balance sheet ready to do a securitisation repayment, and that's undermined the NIM by creating a larger denominator. [The] pathway from here, I can see clear building blocks to get us to that greater than 12% position, and they come from all of the areas that we talked about before. So, the repricing that was completed last year, and flows through into NIM as customers use those cards and pay down the pre-repriced balances. The second thing is the deposits that we talked about previously. Thirdly is just the overall risk mix, clearly we'll get another move on again once we onboard [General Motors] later in the year. The building blocks are still in place, Sheel, so we're comfortable with that progress, it's a really key part of our plan. In terms of Markets VaR, I wouldn't call anything [out] in particular, because it's actually a business style and philosophy across the entirety of the market business. Again, it reflects the strategy that we set out at the beginning of this planning cycle for you, which was a real focus on the fact that we had deployed a lot of technology into the Markets business. That means that we're taking more risk intra-day, not so much in terms of inventory. So that's really the thematic, you could see that across a number of businesses, and it's really a reflection of the investments that we've made. So when I say we've monetised the opportunity within the current environment, that's really what I'm talking about here, and we have been really nimble in the way that we deployed capital. So I wouldn't say anything more specific than that. Thank you.

answer: So, how do we feel about FICC? I would say a couple of things, the first is we are definitely performing better across a range of products. If I go back to some of the periods that you call out, we would not have had the same kind of Securitised Product business, Trading business that we have. Our European Rates business, as we said, has been an area of focus for us. That was very strong historically, we lost market share. We started of focusing on building that market share back through last year, it was definitely a journey through last year and it performed much better in Q1. The other thing I would call out is Fixed Income Financing within here, equally as part of our Financing businesses, are a much more stable source of revenues and Financing in general is a business that we've invested a lot in. We see good balanced growth and robust margins. So I would say the underlying position is objectively good. In any particular quarter, your [comparators] will either help you or weaken your result, that is just the nature of this business. I would say Q1'24 [was] maybe a little bit weaker, but then if you look at the trajectory and exit rate from 2024 into 2025, I think that would take you back towards this stronger position. From our perspective, what we're really focused on is, are those businesses performing well and in the way we would expect them to, [with] the market share as an output. question: But you've called out ECM and M&A, should I interpret that as DCM is more or less business as usual?
answer: No, I don't think it is either, but I think there's sort of event driven pieces and when you get into investment grade, you see the knock on impact there as well, for those event driven pieces. So it's just our concern, if you like, because of the uncertainty, people are just stepping back. But we're not seeing things cancelled, they're just getting pushed out, but it feels like that's an industry impact. In this environment, you tend to see offsetting impact between Banking and Markets. That's certainly what we saw in Q1. So to the extent that volatility suppresses Banking activity, you would expect to see some offset to that in Markets. In terms of RWA efficiency, I'm not going to talk about specific clients. You can see that in Q1, we have less in credit in the IB, and that's being deployed into counterparty credit risk and market risk. So that's what I meant about being nimble with our capital, within the overall framework of the IB. I would say our overall Leverage Finance book is well positioned. We've gone into the current environment probably with low levels of inventory. What we've had has cleared, as we would have expected to, so nothing to call out [in] Markets.

question: Good morning, Venkat and Anna, thanks for taking my questions. Two, please. The first, just focusing on the return targets for 2026. I guess at the halfway point for the strategic plan, the bank's doing better than expected. As Venkat, you mentioned, you've beaten in [Global Markets] six quarters in a row and consensus is pretty close to your £30 billion revenue target for next year. But the market is well over £1 billion below your expectations for the Investment Bank. So I wanted to invite you to sort of give us your thinking on that £30 billion guide. Is it still that number because you're not in the habit of refreshing it every quarter? Is it that the cyclical tailwinds in the IB that you've enjoyed so far you think are a bit of a headwind from here? Because if we put in your IB number, if we add that to consensus, you're a 13% RoTE company, not the sort of more than 12% at which we seem to be a little bit stuck. Secondly, perhaps just as a follow on, consensus beyond 2026 has got the bank growing revenues by 3% and costs by 2%. I wonder whether just at a footprint level, do you think that makes sense? Are the markets in which you're playing growing that little in the next few years? Thanks very much.
answer: Okay, thanks Jason. I'm going to start and then hand to Venkat. So we've retained and indeed repeated our targets for 2025 and for 2026.And when we step back, we're clearly on a strong platform here. At the end of the first half of this year, we're sitting on a 13% RoTE and we clearly got momentum across all five of the businesses. Really, this is what the strategy is about, so we're not surprised by these results. Our objective was to drive income momentum and income stability, whilst holding costs and capital discipline. That's exactly what we're doing here and you can see that in the results. So clearly, what it does is it gives us confidence for the current year. But even more than that, it gives us confidence for 2026 and beyond as a RoTE matter. And income-wise, that being a specific part of your question, what you're seeing here is clear NII momentum, as I covered in the previous conversation. Loan growth will underpin that. You're going to see the maturation of cards balances that will underpin that. You can see the structural hedge underpinning that. Elsewhere in the bank, you can see the progress that we are making structurally in the IB, both as a revenue matter and in terms of a RoTE matter. So, we believe that with each passing quarter, clearly we're more confident and hopefully the market becomes so in that delivery. But it's beyond 2025 and 2026, hopefully you're starting to see a pattern. The strategy is not hard. As I said, it's about driving income momentum and stability, keeping costs controlled, and being really disciplined about where we allocate our capital. We're not going to suddenly stop doing that at the end of 2026. From our perspective, we expect to continue to drive that level of momentum. Venkat, you may want to add. Yes. Look, Jason, you've asked a question or two questions, which really hit at the heart of what our strategy and our strategic plan is. So one is, how well are the businesses performing and how are you getting that better performance? As Anna just said, there's an important part that is structural, we're just trying to run the place much better, with deeper client engagement, greater efficiency in cost, greater revenue growth, strong risk controls. We're very happy with the numbers we've seen over the first six quarters, we think the structural underpinnings, as Anna said, give us expectations to carry that forward, not just into the next six quarters, but beyond that. So one part is running the bank better. The second part comes to the footprint, as you put it, which is what are the businesses and where are they? Now, a large at scale bank like us should grow at top-line roughly at the nominal rate of the economies in which we are. Both in the UK and in the US, that nominal rate, the US is running a 1% GDP growth, real Q4'25 to Q4'24, it's probably going to be 2% next year, with inflation around 4%, call it a 4.5% to 5% nominal growth, similar in the UK. So you would expect us, absent of capturing market share, to grow at roughly that level, is what I would think in the long run a good bank should do. That's not a target, that's not a forecast, it's just saying to you that when you think about how our footprint is, that's a reasonable assumption to start with. Okay thank you Jason. Perhaps we can go to the next question, please.

question: Hi Anna, hi Venkat, thank you for taking my question. Just a couple of quick ones. So on the UK, noted that very clearly [you've] done £10 billion of organic RWA allocation to the business. I guess there is a little bit of nervousness about the UK macro from here. Certainly there is some nervousness around what the autumn budget might have. So in the case that confidence drops off and maybe activity comes down and you find it more difficult to allocate the remaining RWAs to the UK business, do you have a plan B? Would you do acquisition to top it up and make sure you hit £30 billion? And if that's the case, how would you think about that in the context of the £10 billion distribution? So I guess that's number one. Number two, quickly touching on cost. So I think previously you've said that you would expect costs to come down in 2027. I guess it looks like the efficiency savings are coming through as expected, all on track. And if anything, the FX should be a little bit of help as well. So is that still what you would expect maybe closer to £17 billion next year?
answer: Okay. Thank you, Perlie. So we're pleased with the £10 billion organic growth in the UK and you can see from slide 13 that that momentum is picking up, not just in BUK, in the areas that we've talked about before, which is cards and mortgages, [which] we talk about a lot, but also in UK Corporate. So we've had three successive quarters of growth in UK Corporate. And you can actually see BUK Business Banking now starting to turn. And when we set our plan, we focused that plan on areas where we were either underweight or we felt we had opportunities to grow because we'd lost market share. So that's true of, for example, high loan-to-value mortgages, or Corporate and Business Banking, where we have had a much higher loan-to-deposit ratio than our peers in the past. So we remain confident that we can deploy that, noting that we're at a run rate of around £2 billion per quarter in 2025. We're £17 billion at the halfway point. We've got six quarters to go. You can do the math, particularly given that momentum appears to be picking up. So it is, and always has been, an organic plan. And our capital hierarchy, as I said before, remains intact. Number one, regulation. Number two, at least £10 billion. Number three, deploy capital into the UK. So we're not going to compromise on the quality or the returns of that lending in order to meet a target. We're very disciplined. And then on the second question, actually we said it was 2026 when costs would come down. That's still our plan. Our cost income ratio guidance for the full year of this year is 61%. You can see that we've got a strong platform for that from the first half. I just note a couple of things. Firstly, income's a bit seasonal. And secondly, the fact that we did say that we would expect to skew our structural cost actions into the second half of the year. So we've done about £100 million so far. Expect us to be at the top end of the £200 million to £300 million. All of that is contained in the [circa] 61% guidance that we've given you for the cost income ratio. And at this point, we're £1.35 billion through a £2 billion target. So we feel like we've got real momentum, Perlie. So I wouldn't change how we feel about the 2026 cost position. It's a really really key part of the plan and delivering higher returns, more consistent returns. So with that, we will close the call. I'd like to thank you for all of your questions today. We look forward to seeing many of you either on the road over the next few days or indeed on the analyst call next Monday. And if we don't see you, then have a good summer break when it comes. Thank you for that. Thank you.

question: Thank you very much, Chris Hallam from Goldman Sachs. So I guess one simple question, just to begin with, on UK motor, perhaps you could remind us, last quarter you provided some context and overview of your position in that segment, just a recap of that and also how you see the developments over the last 48 hours in terms of impact on the competitive landscape in the UK and also maybe with the potential redress scheme, the sort of growth focus from the UK government. And then secondly, separately, the Investment Bank, you have the 50% of group RWAs target. You have said repeatedly RoTE is the North Star. I think on the call, Jason's question about if the revenue number gets up that would support a higher RoTE outcome for the group. Is that the right way to think about it? That the 50% RWA target would be the one that sort of, you'd be happy to give in order to let the IB do what it can do and probably support outperformance versus targets?
answer: Let me start with UK motor. So just to remind you, we exited the business and sold our business in its entirety in 2019. And up to that point, we'd had a low single digit market share. We were not a big participant in the market. We welcome the clarity and the reduction in uncertainty that's come from the Supreme Court ruling on Friday. And we also welcome the news from the FCA yesterday that they will consult on an industry wide redress scheme. So, we'll be spending time with them and the government ensuring that that is fair and balanced. And that's probably all I can say at this point, you know, given that we've yet to hear from the FCA in detail and, you know, this is live, coming out, but that's broadly where we are. So, nothing really to sort of add from where we've been in the past. On the second point, the 50% is, I would say, both an intent and an output. By an intent, what I mean is it's in service of growing a business with high returns and more stable returns. And that is the simple objective of the plan that we set out. And it's also an output, and it's an output from two really important, if you like, strategic plans within the plan itself. The first is our belief that we have the right waterfront and the right level of capital within the IB. And I think that we've shown that we can grow it and grow its returns within the waterfront that we've given it. And we did say at the outset that we felt there were areas where capital could become more efficient, and we still continue to see that. The second part is clearly the growth in the UK to which we are committed both for the £30 billion [RWA growth] and beyond. You know, we're going to continue to want to grow those high returning businesses. The third piece of the jigsaw, which is less within our control, is clearly the timing of regulatory change. And that's clearly a factor in getting to that 50%. So, the timing of the implementation of the US card model could be 2026/2027 and somewhat out of our hands, Chris. But I think the really important part and the intent is maintaining capital in the IB, certain that we can grow within that and, and continuing to grow the UK group.

question: Phil Richards from Bloomberg Intelligence. Two questions as well please. First of all you have given us quite a lot of information on the structural hedge and the impact on the UK, but if you could just, take a step back and look at the overall UK margin in terms of UK bank and what the outlook is for the next couple of years. And then secondly, credit costs seem to be coming in lower pretty much every quarter, at the moment, than your 50 to 60 base points through the cycle. Is that how you expect it to remain over the next 18 months or so?
answer: So, I'm going to interpret from your question, that you want me to talk about Barclays UK. So I mean we're not guiding to NIM , we're guiding very much to net interest income, and that's really because we're growing both the numerator and the denominator. You know, we're growing our asset businesses, strongly as you can see, and depending, in any particular quarter, the dominance of either secured or unsecured, then that's clearly going to make a difference to that margin from mix. But generally speaking, we do feel we've got momentum in the margin that's coming not just from the structural hedge, and remember that's coming from the strengths of the deposit business overall, but also from the fact that we are growing assets and in particular, I do expect that the promotional balances that we've written over the last 18 months in cards are going to start to mature and they start in the second half of this year. But the, the greater bulk, if you like, the longer dated promotional balances will really pick up in 2026. So, I'm expecting that momentum to continue. But more importantly I would say is just growing the balance sheet overall whilst growing that margin, so you are going to see that continued NII momentum. On credit costs, the UK generally it's just very benign and customers remain very disciplined. We can see that in their actions in terms of their spending. Spending has typically been below inflation for, for some time. We're now seeing signs that credit card spending is outstripping debit card spending but that's a relatively new sort of over the last six months type scenario. And at the same time, through COVID, they very much deleveraged their own balance sheets and we saw quite a reduction in unsecured lending through the UK. So, all of that is going on in the background, but at the same time, you also see real wage growth. You see good demand for mortgages, you know, low, but pretty stable if not slightly growing HPI. So, all of the economic indicators are actually pretty stable. Corporate failures are not systemic, they're idiosyncratic from what we can see. So, there are really no signs of distress in the economy. I mean, to give you an idea, our UK credit card delinquencies across 30 days are 0.7%, and our UK mortgage delinquencies are 0.2% across 90 days. So, they're very, very low in historical standards. So, over time we would expect them to normalise and clearly we're going to see a degree of normalisation as we continue to grow the book. But there's certainly no immediate signs of it so I think the customers are in good shape.

question: Hi, so Jordan from Mediobanca, I had a quick one on US cards. So it was a decent pickup QoQ in the US cards NIM. I was wondering whether that's sort of a new baseline. It's been a bit choppy, that NIM print, as you've had the repricing actions from last year, the changing funding structure. Is this kind of a new benchmark level, we progress from here or is it going to continue to be quite choppy both up and down? And then also there's a bit of complexity in terms of how you book the hedge income within US cards. Just maybe a bit of a better understanding of the nuances there, whether it's through net interest income or other income and [inaudible].
answer: So, we did see progression in the NIM and I expect to see further progression from here. And that's really coming from the repricing actions which continue to mature, as you say, we took them last year, but, customers need to spend on the new terms and conditions for those to become live, and we continue to grow a deposit. We're around 73% [core deposits] now and we expect that to get to over 75%. That's our objective and you can see that on the slide and there is a differential in margin between those broker deposits and direct to retail deposits. Slide 25, if you want to have a look at that. I think it's the chart in the bottom right-hand corner. So, the other thing that's going to help us progress Jordan, is, bringing on GM. So, GM is a higher margin because it's a retail book, but the risk adjusted margin is very good. So, you can see that, remembering Q3, we're going to onboard the back book of GM. We're already originating on the front book, so you're going to see further progress from here I think, in terms of that NIM. And just in terms of the two, quirky things that we've talked about before. We're now starting to book those on a forward basis in a different way. So, you're going to see the hedging come flowing into NII. So previously, the way we hedged this, you saw the margin compression from any rate reduction coming through in the NIM and you saw the offsetting income in non- NII. You're now going to see those geographically in the same place, bringing it into alignment with the group. And the third thing is, whilst it's not a massive matter in the quarter, previously what we've done is where we've had large pools of cash on the balance sheet used to pay down securitisation, they were included in that NIM calculation on an ongoing basis. Again, in alignment with the group, we will exclude those. So, I think some of that will take some of the choppiness that you've seen quarter to quarter out of the NIM also, Jordan. But the, most important thing is this forward momentum that's going to come from pricing and mix really. Okay, thank you.

question: Good morning. Thank you for taking my questions. The first one, just looking at competitive conditions in US Investment Banking, we've had some of the peers talk about potentially very significant levels of additional capital that's available for deployment following some of the deregulation and stress test changes. And Prime appears to be one of the places that they may be looking to allocate additional capacity. So, given it's a focus for the bank, could you just talk about whether you think you have additional capital to deploy given the changes in things like stress tests and what you're seeing on product margins and that sort of thing? And then secondly, on the non-bank financial intermediary (NBFI) space, thank you for the additional disclosures. Those are really welcome and it's good to see the impairment charge at a group level below consensus today. Venkat, I wonder whether you could talk a little bit about risks in that industry, how mature the exposures are, whether there are any vintages we should be bothered about. We could observe that the cases we've seen so far all involve fraud, but we have seen very strong growth in the industry writ large. And so, I wonder with your risk management hat on, whether you could just talk about, whether this is an industry that has yet to grind into fully mature loss run rates and how you think about that sort of thing. Thank you.
answer: All right. Thank you Jason for both questions. On the first one on capital regulation or disparity, potential disparity in capital regulation between Europe, the UK and the US. Look, it is, I think, an important factor in the industry. We haven't seen ultimately what will be the changes in the US and how much the UK, which is the important jurisdiction for us as a home regulator, makes itself consistent or not. I think what I would point out on things like Prime is, we've got a good and strong market share. We work with a few important and big clients carefully. It is as much a balance sheet business as it is a capital business. And so, we think we've got the wherewithal, and given our current market position, given our product capability, given our client penetration, we've got the wherewithal to compete effectively and continue to compete effectively. Of course, it's all subject to capital rules. We'll have to see where they are, but I'm pretty confident in the strength of that business and how we will adapt overall in the Investment Bank, because ultimately, it's about that. Coming back to private credit and NBFI, so here's what I will say. First of all, I view credit as credit as credit, right? There's a distinction about where it's originated from, and you know, private credit, generally, we at least think of it as the kind of credit that's originated outside of banks and outside of the public debt market. But I think of lending as lending, and through the cycle, you've got to be careful about all the aspects of lending. Client selection, sector concentrations, NIM concentrations, terms, and continuous monitoring, qualifying them initially and monitoring it over the time period. So that's important, and that you've got to do through the period. I'm obviously disappointed that we had Tricolor. The fact that it was fraud is no excuse. We have looked at what lessons we can learn from that and apply that across our portfolios. I will talk a little about that. We did not have First Brands. We were approached a couple of times, and we said no. We said no because our credit officers felt that there was not enough data information to support the financial projections they made. That's how credit selection is supposed to work. Now, at this point in time, and you talk a little about vintages. Less to me a question about vintage, but two questions, one is are there circumstances either because of inflation, tariffs or changes in general economic conditions that put stress on credit performance. So, do companies find themselves stretched? Now fraud can be isolated bad actors, or it could be economic conditions that increase the propensity towards bad acting. And then if you worry about that, you've got to consider very carefully the independence and strength of the financial controls employed within the companies. Now as you can imagine, we consider all of these things over time. But I think what these two instances show is that we will likely be monitoring our portfolios more carefully, particularly understanding the impact of changed economic conditions on companies and looking closely at the strength and independence of financial controls. Hope that answers your question. Thanks.

question: Good morning. Thanks for taking my questions. Just on private credit again, could you help us with the economics of how that business works? So what spread are you making on the business, the risk weights? I presume it's been growing very quickly. Are you worried that if the Bank of England, I mean regardless of how confident and low risk your particular book is, are you worried that if the Bank of England is looking into it, it's going to deter you from further growth in that area? And then in Kensington in the UK, I see you've doubled the book, so that makes around £4 billion now, if I'm not mistaken. Do you have any desire to go into any other areas of specialised lending in the UK? Thanks.
answer: Right. Let me take the first one, Rob, and then Anna will cover Kensington. So, we have a disclosure slide, slide 43 in our [Q325 Results Presentation] on private credit. What I would say is that the exposure is growing in a sort of relatively stable manner and has been for us for a while. I'm not going to get into RWAs and spreads. I think we've been very clear about the strong credit controls we put on this and the types of people we work with. To reiterate, we work with the most experienced, well-regarded, top-notch, top players in the industry. We provide financing generally against pools of loans, of credits which they originate on a secured basis. Those portfolios are diversified. We have limits on borrower concentration and sector concentrations. We are skewed towards large-cap corporates. We require lower LTVs so that we can get better first-class protection, and we've got some statistics there, and we retain revaluation rights, which means mark-to-market rights on the portfolio and enforce the maintenance of LTVs, and collateral additions require our individual approval. So, it's a risk management process and practice. I think it's important that regulators examine all aspects of the financial system. We welcome the review by the Bank of England, and as I said, that we've got strong risk management practices. So, we're comfortable and confident in that. Thanks, Venkat. Rob, on your question on Kensington, the balances are around £4 billion in Kensington. Just to sort of highlight how we think about this business, I mean, it's no different actually in risk management terms, to the way Venkat's just described private credit or indeed any kind of credit. So, we're very focused on the choice of customers, so Kensington has 30 years of experience of really focused client and product level afordability assessments. And then once the balances are on our balance sheet then we do manage them actively and that was one of the capabilities that we drew from Kensington. So, you might have noticed that in Q3, we actually did a Stage 3 securitisation from there. So, it is quite a sophisticated risk capability, and it is contributing not only to the breadth of mortgage ff o ering but also to the blended margin. But thank you for the question. Next question, please.

question: Good morning. Just a couple of questions. First on distribution. So, I think it's very welcome to see a buyback this quarter and moving to quarterly distributions. Can you just tell us how you thought about it? Why did you decide to go to quarterly cadence? And in terms of going forward, is there a sort of monthly rolling number that you are thinking about? And within the wider distribution context, now that [your shares are trading closer to 1x] price to book, are you thinking about maybe [doing a different mix of distributions, including more dividends?]. So that's number one. Number two is on cost. You highlighted that you've achieved your efficiency savings one quarter earlier than expected. But also, for next quarter, you would expect to run towards the top end of the £200 to £300m SCAs, if you like. So is that something that you would expect to run at that level in 2026? And as part of the strategy update, I think last time we did it, I think there was maybe £900 million or £1 billion SCAs up front as well. Is that something that you are thinking about as well?
answer: Thanks, Perlie. Let me take both of those. So the buyback decision, really what that reflects is our confidence in the consistency of generation of capital, and it's just a clear articulation of the capital priorities that we gave you at the outset of the plan, which were number one, you should expect us to be well capitalised as a regulatory matter. Number two, returning capital to shareholders, and number three, investing in the businesses. So, as we reflected over the last few quarters, we've seen the strength and quality and resilience of that capital generation, this is something that we've been thinking about. So, what we've done is we've accelerated a portion that we would otherwise have paid at the full year, and that's really our desire to put it in the hands of shareholders. So, nothing more significant than that. In terms of the go forward plan, in terms of balance, cadence, et cetera, we will cover that with you in February when we give you those target updates. In terms of costs. So, our primary objective here is to continue to drive efficiencies. That's what we're doing, and our structural cost actions play a really key role in driving that forward. But there's no real change here at all, and in fact, given the delivery of [our FY25 gross efficiencies target] a quarter early, and given we've got such momentum in our NII, had it not been for motor finance, I would have been expecting today to upgrade the cost to income ratio to around 60%. As it is, given that progress, we've been able to absorb motor finance and reiterate our 61% guidance to you. I still expect next year to be in the high-50s. Typically, in any year, we spend between £200 million and £300 million [on SCAs]. That's what we're guiding you to this year. We're just calling out it might be towards the top end of that, but again, that is all encapsulated within the guidance that we've given you of circa 61% for this year. There's no real change to anything that we are saying in terms of costs. But thank you for the question. Perhaps we could go to the next question, please.

question: Thanks very much. Good morning, everybody. I just had a question on your 2026 targets, actually, because if I look across the piece, I mean, you're pretty much nailing every one and some by some margin, but I guess the one that stands out is the Investment Bank RWAs, which I can see you've reiterated today at 50%, which is still quite a long way from where we are today. And I'm just thinking that in terms of the returns, they are significantly below the other divisions. And I would hazard that the cost of equity is higher as well, and I guess that's probably the division which is the reason for you trading where you do. So, I do think that 50% is quite an important target, particularly in terms of a statement of intent and where we see it going from there. But I don't really see how you're going to get there. And so can you give us sort of some flavor are we talking about a big reduction in Investment Bank RWAs? Is it some sort of risk transfer you're going to do? Or are we looking at much bigger growth somewhere that I'm not thinking about? Because you're talking about more than a 10% swing there. Thanks very much.
answer: Okay, Ed, why don't I start and then I'll hand to Venkat. So just in terms of the 50%, remember, when we wrote that, we were in a very different environment in terms of regulatory timing. So, there are two things that are under our control and one that isn't. The first is holding the Investment Bank RWAs flat. We've actually done that for more than three and a half years now. It's not just part of this strategy, it was there before. Secondly, continuing through in the UK and you can see the progress. The thing that I can't control is the implementation date of the IRB model or indeed, some of the Basel implementation effects. But the strategic intent that sits underneath that 50% remains the same, Ed, but there's regulatory timing that I can't control. As to your point on returns, I mean, we were really clear that the returns of the Investment Bank were not where they needed to be, but you can see that we're making progress. Just to call it out, it's 12.9% year-to-date, much more in line with the Group versus 10.1% last year. So, we are making good progress, but I'll hand to Venkat for more comments. Yes, look, I'll say exactly that. We were very, very clear at the start of our strategy that we were going to hold the Investment Bank RWAs flat. And the reasoning behind that was we felt and we feel we've got a very strong, capable full Investment Bank, and that at those levels of RWA, with greater RWA efficiency, which we've demonstrated, can be very competitive. And we've shown our competitiveness over the long time, over this period. What we said also was that the percentage is an outcome, as Anna just described, which is based on not just holding it flat, but growing in the UK, and then assumptions about capital calculations for the rest of our book, particularly US Cards. The first two we control, holding the Investment Bank RWAs flat, and then what we've been doing in the UK, where we've been showing the growth, which we said we would. The third part we cannot control, and that affects the percentage. And if you go beyond that. The flat is exactly the important point. And as Anna said, on RoTE, it's again been behaving exactly the way we would want, it's a returns focused business. And it is approaching, and in some instances, if you look at the time periods of the past, the Group average. So exactly what was outlined, exactly what has been delivered, the promise is kept. Thank you very much, everybody. Thank you. Thank you, everybody. Thank you, Ed, for that question. We will see you on the road from tomorrow, and we are looking forward to an analyst lunch as opposed to an analyst breakfast next Tuesday. So, I hope to see you all soon, and thank you for your continued interest in Barclays. Thank you. Thank you.

question: Starting with the Best Egg transaction, can you help us a bit on the cost and the impairment side of things? So, does that mean impairment is also going to be quite low [versus revenues]? Number two, I know the 2028 target is something that you would not want to talk too much about right now. With the Best Egg transaction, we have greater visibility as to how we can get to mid-teens for the business, and then the UK businesses, all three of them are easily making greater than 20%. question: Thank you for taking my questions. I've got a slightly out the picture question if that's okay. Stablecoins, just being something we've been talking about recently. I think Barclays has previously spoken about its use case in the wholesale market and I think one of your peers, Lloyds, has commented on the deposit usage in retail business. But the disclosure has been quite limited, I guess the topic's quite new. Just interested to hear your views on [what the direction of travel is], in terms of maybe costs or timeline or any regulatory challenges? Ultimately do you think it's going to make a material difference for Barclays and your clients?
answer: Dan's been very involved in this. I think it's obviously a very interesting topic for us to watch. I mean, at the moment, I think the stablecoin use case has primarily been crypto, of-ramp, on-ramp and some remittance activity. I think sort of take up more broadly across international payments with corporates has still been relatively limited, but I think that's where we see that it could have potential for further application. I think the use case in retail is much less clear. It's obviously something that we will we'll watch closely, but for a couple of reasons. Firstly, I think the definition of stablecoin as money is still somewhat lacking, in confidence and security. Secondly, the use case in terms of the fact that retail domestic payments are already pretty straightforward to do. So I think the use case for retail is much less clear. So we'll watch this space really closely. As you know, there's been a press release on it, we're engaging with the other UK banks on testing some of these technologies. And we'll be testing use cases there, both in the wholesale space and also in the retail space. But the retail space, less stablecoin and more about adding features to the existing form of money. So we'll be testing those, so a lot to watch, I think.

question: The first on the Private Bank, on NII, which was down in the quarter, with increase in deposit balances. So just thinking about going forward, if this is a start of a trend or if there are some one ofs or things going on in the quarter in particular. So, broadly happy with it, but it has somewhat eroded the NII in the quarter. We'd expect a broadly similar level of income I think as we head into Q4, but just a reflection, I guess, of the nature of the clients. Just to remind you, I mean, that is a very, very high RoTE business and it remains above the target of greater than 25% that we've given you for 2026. So if I go into the UK Corporate Bank, we've seen really good income growth there, there's nothing in particular as a single matter I would call out. Just deposit growth and lending growth fundamentally coming through into that top line into the NII.

question: Two questions please. First, coming back to Best Egg, because it isn't a bank and it's clearly being acquired by a bank. Would the rules have to change with regards to holding an equity slice, or a tranche of the securitisations? Could you speak to maybe how that works, for Barclays? Then secondly, looking at the SRT book, I know you haven't given disclosure for the third quarter, but for the second quarter, it's declined about £7 billion. So, I'm just wondering, is that a timing issue or how should we think about that, and how does that tally with the capital efficiency in the Investment Bank?
answer: In terms of Best Egg, you're right, it's not a bank, it does become part of one as this transaction completes. There are implications of that in terms of its funding. Obviously creates some efficiencies. In terms of the regulatory requirements around the slice that it holds, I don't believe that they are significantly different, but we can revert. But I don't believe so, Dan may want to add to that. So, from our perspective, given its business model and given the way we are already embedded in that business model in the Investment Bank, actually we see efficiencies here, because we have the pre-securitisation funding opportunity. We clearly have reduced securitisation costs because there are things that we will be doing in house. We have an ability also to have a flow of consumer credit into that ABS business. So, from our perspective, it's a net benefit in that particular part. Dan, SRT? There's a very consistent level of activity in SRT, so there's nothing I would call out. Maybe we can follow up with you afterwards on whether there's FX or amortisation. There are numbers, but the footprint has been very, very consistent. Again, that's sort of consistent with what we've said before. We do see that Colonnade program in particular as being a mature program and we manage it carefully in terms of its reinvestment cadence. So, I think it's probably in the detail rather than anything deliberate.

question: On Best Egg, in terms of the financials here, you've given us the high single digit P/E of something like a £90 million bottom line. I think you've indicated that the ROIC (Return on Invested Capital) is going to be commensurate with the UK businesses, if I've understood you correctly. So, £90m [bottom line] versus your £800m investment seems to imply quite a meaningful amount of cost synergy that you expect to deliver over time. I'm just mindful of that implying potentially a step up in costs in USCB as we look into 2026. I'm just curious if you could give us an indication of the cost base that's attached to this. Appreciate you've sort of indicated the revenues are commensurate with the American Airlines book, but just in terms of the cost, that would be helpful, I think for our modelling. Then in terms of the longer-term capital allocation question, it came up on the call last week. There's obviously market sensitivity around your 50% Investment Bank allocation target. I guess the $40 billion end net receivables target [in USCB], you weren't necessarily expecting quite so much of it to be servicing relationships when you set out the strategic plan. So, the $16 billion card IRB impact, it would just be scaling that down by $4-5 billion for the fact that, out of the $40 billion of targeted balances, over a quarter is now of-balance sheet and therefore presumably be not impacted at all by IRB.
answer: You're sort of broadly at the right sort of earnings level. I think as an ROI matter, what we're saying is in time you're right, we do expect to grow the earnings of this business, and I would say probably in the following order. Starting with funding synergies. Again, remember that's what we did in Tesco, they're the ones that normally come through first and I called those out before. Remember, this isn't a bank at the moment. So, there are clear funding synergies in terms of the pre-securitisation position, the cost of securitisation itself. Then you come to cost synergies, for a while we would expect to run this as a business in parallel and then incur the integration over time. So I wouldn't call out any particular integration chunks next year, but clearly, we'll update you on that. But funding is a key point. And I also think those revenue synergies are going to come from a number of different places. So, as I said before, it's cross selling cards and deposits to customers who come to us via Best Egg. It's going in the opposite direction and extending the Best Egg capability across all of our partners into the cards business. It's also actually about our ability to create a forward flow of consumer business into our Investment Bank, so that's also important here. I think funding, revenue and costs will come in time, but we do have confidence that we can get this to high teens RoTE. On the Investment Bank, clearly when we set that 50% [target] out, there was an expectation of timing of regulatory change, and that's clearly changed over time. That $16 billion was therefore related to a level of balances that was not $40 billion. So I think that's the first thing to remember, because we expected to go through AIRB actually in 2025, it seems like quite a long time ago, but I'm sure our original expectation was 2025, by which time the balances would not have been $40 billion. So, I wouldn't necessarily do the kind of scaling that that you're talking about here. That said, you are right, we've replaced capital heavy balances with capital light balances. Although we'll retain a small portion of the loans, the AIRB treatment of loans is relatively much lower than it is for cards. So you're not really going to see a material step change there, both because of the nature of the change and also because of the quantum. But the 50%, or the spirit behind the 50%, remains intact, which was about holding the Investment Bank [RWAs] flat. You should expect us to continue to do that and expect us to continue to grow the UK in particular. And it was really the UK growth that was driving that change. The regulatory change is timing and at the point where we have a better estimate of that $16 billion, we will of course come to you with it. But unfortunately, the quantum and the timing has some regulatory uncertainty around that.

question: I wanted to ask about the Financing Business, please. I mean, that's been working well for you. As Dan said earlier, you've been focused on the largest of the hedge funds. But, from what we can see, and I think disclosure across the industry isn't very good here, but from what we can see, your penetration into those very largest hedge funds is now approaching the kind of top three Financing firms to the big US banks. But where you have less penetration is in kind of the next rung down. Is there still a lot more scope, you think to increase penetration further and really kind of catch up or maybe even overtake the biggest players in the industry among that top group of hedge funds? Or are you going to have to start focusing more on the next rungs down?
answer: Our Financing business is working well and remember this comes in two parts. So, our Fixed Income Financing business, very much embedded in the heritage of Barclays and Lehman before it. It is typically number one or two in the market. So very, very well-established business. What we've been doing is growing Prime alongside that. We've gone from typically number seven or eight to joint number five. So, we've clearly made some progress there. As you note, our targeting has been with the larger of the hedge funds, that's deliberate, and it reflects both our business model and our view of risk. So by business model, what I mean is we run our Financing business as an integrated business. So Fixed Income Financing and Prime are run under a single leadership. So when we approach a client, that's how we approach them, not as two individual businesses. We also run our technology that way. So, as we're looking at those clients, we look across their business in its totality, and we believe that gives us a better perspective of their risk. That lends itself to the largest global multi-strategy type funds, so that's really why you see that approach. But also, in terms of our own risk positioning, we do believe that, again, the first step in risk management is through the careful selection of clients, and therefore we choose to work with the larger, more capitalised, more liquid clients in the industry. That's really where we prefer to operate. That may mean that we give up a little margin along the way, but that certainly is a risk matter where we would want to operate. So, it's a deliberate strategy. So, from our perspective, we would want to grow as they do. Clearly, we do feel there's more for us to do there. Thank you so much. Really appreciate you coming in again on a very busy day in the market. So, appreciate your time and questions, particularly on Best Egg. We will see you on the 10th of February, if not before. Thank you very much.

question: Two questions. The first question is on the capital return of over £15 billion. If you could just put this in context of capacity to support investment and growth. How should we think about this capacity that you're outlining? It looks like there's quite a bit of buffer. So we would like to understand that. And then secondly, you're one of the few CEOs who actually discusses ledgers and middle office integration, which is not a hot topic. Just what the focus is and how should we think about post 2028 basically in that respect?
answer: Anna, do you want to start on the capital and then we can come back to the other one? Sure. Thanks, Kian. So one of the hallmarks of this plan is the level of capital generation. We've talked about that. And really when we talk about an improving profit signature, that's really what we mean. It's this chart here that they've just brought up showing that sort of change to 230 basis points. (slide 71) And in the plan, what we've done is we've meaningfully increased the distribution to greater than £15 billion, but we've also meaningfully, in fact doubled the level of investment. But such is the level of capital generation within the plan. The level of generation actually surpasses both of those two increases. What we've done here is we've deliberately created some capacity for us to be able to invest further if and only if we determine that is the right thing for us to do. And I'll just remind you of our very clear capital hierarchy here and specifically the importance of shareholder returns. So, we're going to set a very, very high bar for any additional level of investment. And quite frankly, if we are unable to find such an investment, then the capital hierarchy will kick in and we will distribute more than we have here in the plan or alternatively, we will be investing more than we have here in the plan and we would expect the momentum of the business in the outer years to be higher than we're presenting here. You know, it comes from both a philosophical place and from the actual reality of the business. The philosophical place is, as I said, for a long time in this industry, the technology has revolved around the businesses. Now, as you see not just in us, but across the industry, the depth and extent of technology-based services, products, and delivery, the businesses are evolving around technology. And what that means, especially if you're going to take advantage of the promise of new technologies like AI and cloud computing is that you've really got to, harmonise your processes and standardise your approaches. And especially when it comes to data platforms and to the way in which you construct and store your data, the way in which you do computing, the way in which you build models and the way in which you deliver. question: One of them is kind of a follow-up to the second question maybe for you, Venkat. In one of the slides and you pointed out that 75% of the employees are in support functions. question: So on the Investment Bank, if I look at your 2026 targets, previously you had a greater than 12% target. It's now circa 12%, a high-50s cost income ratio is now circa 60%. I'm assuming the change is primarily due to FX, but perhaps you could firstly confirm? Secondly, when I go back two years and think of the original plan, a lot of the revenue growth was assumed to come from market share gains and you actually assumed a fairly flat wallet. Actually, what's materialised is a much better wallet than you expected, but flat market share. So perhaps you could also just talk to competitive dynamics and how that's played out versus what you thought two years ago and how that then fed through to your 2028 assumptions as well. Then on the US Consumer Bank, I just wanted to understand some of the moving parts because you talked about greater than 13% NIM for 2026 full year, but I think in your earlier commentary, you said 12.5% for Q1, 14% for the second half post the [American Airlines] sale. So, presuming it's the 14% you would argue we should be thinking about into the outer years. So that movement in FX is worth about 50 basis points. So, all we're doing is we're just truing up our expectations. We're pleased with the progress that it's made so far. I'm not going to mark-to-market that plan every single passing quarter. It's just that as we're resetting targets, we felt like it was the appropriate thing to do. Thank you. I think, on the other side, what I would point to is, on the Investment Bank side, Banking per se, as I said to you, we would like to see greater fee share. What you've seen so far is progress from the hires and the investments we've made, and you've seen greater revenues, obviously and excellent capital discipline. So roughly speaking, it's not much more to the Investment Bank and the cost guidance at a Group level only modestly growing from now to 2028. That suggests [the] Investment Bank not getting very much cost either. answer: So how do we think about product margin in the UK is I think your question. So, look, there's a bit more to go here and you can see that from the, can we go to the structural hedge slide, please? Thank you. (slide 64). We are assuming that we are going to be reinvesting the structural hedge at 3.5%. The maturing yield over the next three years is materially below that. So, 1.5%, 2.1%, 2.7%. So, you're going to have a considerable hedge tailwind across at least this plan, probably beyond. And everything that we've done around the tenure of the hedge and extending it from 3% to 3.5% is only going to increase that momentum for longer. So that remains there as a, if you like an underpin for product margins. Then if you think about lending more and particularly within our credit card business, all of the volume that we've written over the last two years coming to maturity from its promotional balances, that will start to increase the interest-earning lending in the credit card book. question: I've got two, please. Anna, can you talk about your thoughts on kind of deposit volumes and spreads in Barclays UK, please. So, we saw a pickup in volumes after a few quarters of kind of flat to slightly down. And I think as well, your UK NII guidance kind of implicitly assumes quite a bit of deposit pressure. So, is that migration, is it product spread pressure? Then Venkat, just back on the Investment Bank, I mean, it sounds like you're very theoretically open to putting more investment in there, but what actually has to happen? So, the revenue on risk-weighted assets has gone up. You're talking about a 13% plus RoTE. How much higher do those numbers have to go before you think you'll give this business another £20 billion of risk-weighted assets?
answer: Okay. So, on UK deposits, you can see that the deposits are up quarter-on-quarter by around £3 billion if we go to this slide. (Slide 17). What we can continue to see there, James, is we do continue to see some competitive pressure in the UK and specifically that move towards fixed or time deposits. Now, seasonally, I would expect some concentration of that in Q1, Q2 just because of the ISA season in the UK. We always see that and it feels like as a market, we're well primed to see that. But we are pleased with that deposit progress. What does that underpin? Well, I think just continued improvements in the business. And I would say that we've deployed our multi brands in deposits this year. We don't really talk about that. We talk about it a lot in assets, but you know, we are going to market with a much more sophisticated product architecture in deposits because we are now deploying the Tesco brand here. So that's really helping us. But we are not assuming from here that there is any real easing in that deposit environment. It may happen, it may not. But as I say, we're trying not to make significant market assumptions. Yeah. So, on the Investment Bank, first of all, investment comes in different ways. Investment comes in people, investment comes in technology, particularly in the Markets business and then investment can come in RWAs. What we've spoken about on the balancing side is basically Investment Bank RWAs as a percentage of the Group, where we set a target of around 50% seems right. We've also indicated flexibility around that number if there's a little opportunity, but 50% seems right. We have been investing heavily on technology and people, and we've spoken about it, whether it's bankers, whether it's trading capability and of course, electronic trading capability. We spoke a little earlier about the investments we've made in Prime. So, there's been and continues to be tremendous investment in technology and capability. Some of this or a lot of it is going towards things that are relatively capital-light and relatively high in fees. We are prioritising stable income, we are prioritising Corporate Banking and of course, electronic trading, which helps with our Intermediation. And on the capital side, as I've said, there is a balancing act and it's about 50% is where we would aim to target. And to get there right now, Investment Bank RWAs have to be relatively flat.

question: Just a quick one for me. At the beginning of the remarks, you mentioned UK is more of an incumbent in terms of AI, while in the US, it's more of a disruptor. So, if we're thinking further down the line, which one of the two parts is the most sustainable in that regard. You're thinking being in the US as a disruptor makes sense, would that open risks for the UK from potential disruptors? And how would you react to that?
answer: Good question. Thank you. We do think of ourselves on either side of the Atlantic, certainly in retail terms as different things. And originally started as the card business in the US, but now what you've seen is us adding a digital savings platform and now digital unsecured lending. So, pulling that together and being very partner-focused with a broad representation. So, it's not a bricks-and-mortar business. Interestingly, and I don't think we talk about this so much, bigger than Chase in the UK. It's a substantial business. And we do see opportunities to grow it with that sort of framework in mind. So very digitally led. In the UK, we start from a very different place. In UK Corporate or in Barclays UK, you're talking about very, very strong primary banking relationships, which, as you say, is where I started this discussion. So, you're really trying to bring your customer or your client into your ecosystem and do as much for them as possible. That's very different from the kind of disruptive mindset. We see our strategy from here as being very much a continuation of that. That said, in the UK, it's really important that the app and the pricing are as good as those of our competitors and indeed our customer service. We've made a lot of progress over the last few years. We're now pretty much top of the large banks in terms of customer service, but we don't recognise that as the standard that we need to get to because of some of the disruptors around us. I think of it as remaining true to being a disruptor in the US and in the UK using the disruptive elements around you to make your primary relationship better and better and better.

question: My questions are more on the AI sort of CapEx cycle and if you could help us think through it. So, some of the plans in the US of the hyperscalers have humongous sort of numbers behind on the CapEx side, which, I mean, it looks good for business, issuance, etc, presumably deal logic suggests that year-to-date, things are going very, very well. But on the other side, we see a lot of the banks offloading data centre risk and some of these numbers, the share price reaction questioning if it's a good use of money. How are you thinking about it from an underwriting perspective? Are you just intermediating, issuing, helping them issuing the bonds? Or how much risk are you taking from a credit perspective? Or how are you thinking about it? And potentially on the other side, more as you think further down the line as well on the underwriting risk, how do you think about AI affecting the underwriting risk more broadly? I'm thinking also here on the retail side, the risk of disruption sort of efficiencies and ultimately would lead to job losses. Can you help us think through it because that's also doing the round.
answer: So let me start with sort of AI / software just as an Investment Bank matter. I mean we don't think of this as differently to other sectors really. So, expect us - and I think it's Slide 100 in the deck, expect us to deal with this type of credit with the same degree of rigor, even though it's had clearly a huge strategic focus, there is a massive sort of build in funding in the US. From our perspective, we would maintain the same kind of concentration limits, the same kind of sector diversification requirements as we would have anywhere else, both in terms of the sector and the counterparties involved. Expect us to deal with parties that are relatively larger and more established, etc. So just a continuation of that really. If we had significant concentrations, you would see it in our disclosures, and you can see that actually it's subsumed within a much larger bucket, the name which I've completely forgotten, but we will come back to you. So it's not an outsized position for us. That said, given the activities over the last sort of four to six weeks, we are extremely focused on it and extremely focused on the levels of risk. And obviously, here, we use SRT as we use elsewhere in other sectors. So, nothing to call out if there were, then we would have done so. In terms of underwriting on personal, we've had some really interesting questions on the road on this actually as to whether or not we should be expecting more of a white-collar recession versus a blue-collar recession, particularly in the US. But we see no movement in credit thus far. We're obviously very watchful as we always are, both in the UK and in the US. It feels a bit early to call the shape of the impact from many of our competitors and many firms across the industry, they're not really talking about headcount reduction. They're really talking about the spending that they're undertaking and perhaps technology efficiency. So, we will watch it very, very carefully. We're also very mindful that AI and sort of data more generally can bring us huge benefits on the underwriting side just because of our ability to ingest data and process that data. That's actually the fundamental basis of Best Egg. So, we do see opportunities to learn here. I think it's on both sides of that particular argument, Alvaro, but very, very watchful.

question: If we could stick with Best Egg for a moment. You spoke about bringing the data sort of expertise to other partners or perhaps I was thinking more RWA efficiency gains and so on. So, if you could just talk a little bit about what that might mean and if there are consequences for post Basel IRB RWA density, perhaps where you think that might land once all that's done. Secondly, in the strategy slides, there's quite a lot of talk about the huge growth you've seen in Prime balances and there's interest in the market as to what's happening to margins there. So, if you wouldn't mind just sort of repeating what's happened to balances and revenues, where they live and how you're seeing things evolve in that part of the Investment Bank, that would be great.
answer: Best Egg comes from two things really. The first is our desire to be this more sort of rounded consumer disruptor, if you like, in the US. So really looking for a capability around unsecured loans. We were doing some unsecured lending with some of our partners, but it was really quite limited. So really, if you like, purchasing a capability that we really lacked. So it's partly about the products there, but equally about the capital-light model. Now unsecured loans are lower in capital anyway, even under IRB than cards because obviously, it's fully drawn. There's no undrawn element to it. So, it's an inherently more capital-efficient product even if you keep it on your balance sheet. But obviously, the nature of Best Egg is it's a largely originated securitised model. So, from that perspective, we are really mindful of the impact of IRB and potentially the regulatory divergence that we have versus some of our US peers. And therefore, the strategy for this business was both to diversify and to look for more capital-light streams of revenue. And if you recall, way back in 2024, we did that very early trade in terms of securitising the credit card balances. So, I expect us to lean on both things on both the diversification and the capital-light nature of it. We expect to bring cards and savings and Best Egg to our partners. Sort of simultaneously, if you like, so a much fuller relationship for them. We do expect to securitise much of what we are doing in the US. And that's also very attractive because it means that we're originating consumer lending for our markets business, which gives benefits there also. So, it's quite a fulsome integrated strategy if that makes sense.

question: I've got two questions, please. First, on the Investment Banking business. You've done a review of the loan book, so 60% of that is done, and you've seen a 150 basis points pickup in income over RWAs. Firstly, can I ask how much of that pickup is due to maybe more penetration on the income side versus the recycling on the RWA side? And secondly, on the remaining 40% how much of a benefit should we expect? Are we thinking that the low-hanging fruit is already done and we're going to be squeezing harder? Or should it be a sort of a symmetrical benefit there? And then secondly, on UK corporates, a lot of these banks in the UK are targeting this segment. Can I ask how asset spreads are looking in this market, particularly as market share gains is a story for a lot of the banks here?
answer: So the answer is it's a bit of a combination, and we haven't split that out because essentially, what we are doing here is we recognise that two things were true, and they're drawn from, if you like, our historic strength in Fixed Income across Barclays very, very widely. So we're very good at DCM, very good at Lending, probably not as disciplined as we should have been around the returns on that Lending and very focused on getting the initial piece of debt, the RCF and then assuming that we would get subsequent Banking fees to go with us with that, and that would complete the client returns. Clearly, that's quite difficult for us to control. It didn't always happen, which is one of the reasons we pushed more discipline into that business. So, it's not only about reviewing the returns of those loans as they come up for renewal, but also saying what happens then? Either the returns have to improve or we have to broaden the relationship out into Transaction banking. So it's actually a combination of the we see it as one single discussion with the client, which is why we haven't separated it. But we have seen considerable growth in deposit balances. I want to say our dollar deposits are up by about 140%. And that reflects the particular focus we had on, if you like, our US or US nexus clients. So, they might be UK businesses operating in the US, we might have some dollar debt with them. We also want to have some dollar deposits. So, I would say a combination of the two. The remaining 40%, don't think of it as low-hanging fruit. Think of it as literally the things that came up for renewal during that period. Roughly, the loans have a three-year average life. So, there's no reason to expect that the remaining year will be different to the first two is the way I would think about it. In terms of UK Corporate Banking, so what we haven't seen there is a compression in asset spreads. And from our perspective, it's really because we were coming from way behind. So, we are still considerably below our natural market share in that business. So, our loan-to-deposit ratio is 34%. If you look at our peers, it's going to be anywhere between 55% and 80%. So, we're coming from a really different position. And all we've done is created an expectation that we would lend with the regional teams and improve the process. Now clearly, we would expect to see some momentum there also coming from the fact that we're consolidating everything onto one platform from five in the shape of Portal. But as I look, I'm really happy to see the growth. They've grown their income in the fourth quarter by 18% from lending. We've seen about 100 basis point pickup in market share. I'm really happy about that, but I'm just as focused on the RoTE, which means there's two things that matter. The first is the default grade. The second is the margin. And neither of those two things are moving relative to the portfolio. So, this is not an expansion driven by pricing and risk. It's an expansion driven by capability and willingness to lend with clients we already have in the door. And indeed, going out and getting new clients. So, we've got, I think, more than 1,100 new clients in just two years. So, the business has some momentum now that it has not had for years. And actually, as I look sort of further out in the plan, one of the areas where I think probably consensus and our expectations are a little bit departing is probably the corporate business.

question: Thanks for your comments on AI within the deposit book. There's an awful lot of first, as you say, from the challenger banks for the deposits, a lot of term deposit compression, instant access savings compression. AI is kind of building the tech there, even though we've had open banking for ages, it only seems to just be impacting the market. What are the sort of the chances that, that level of deposit spread compression persists forever? And the NII actually comes out at £8.1 billion and flat lines because it's just expensive to run in the deposit market, and this just gets perpetually chipped away by technology. And then secondly, kind of on AI as well, just what impact you see it having in the wealth market, given that's a bit of a focus last week and kind of looking at the reaction that the market has had and investors had to NatWest Evelyn. Does that make you question the reaction that people have had, does that make you question any acquisitions in wealth now?
answer: Thank you, Rob. Well, Vim Maru was reminding me yesterday that the first such platform was launched by Bradford and Bingley some time ago. So, this kind of approach has been out there for some time. We've obviously seen it become more sophisticated. But customers are moving their deposits around now. It's pretty much a friction-free market because we're nearly all optimising our deposits on our app, and it's pretty easy to do. That said, we are not seeing a significantly higher level of term deposits than we saw immediately post crisis. So there seems to be a sort of natural level, if you like. That said, we can't rely on that, which is why we're investing so much in the app because actually, what you want to do is bring your customers into your environment and for them to find everything that they need there so that they don't need to go. And obviously, that means that you know them better because you have the primary banking relationship, you can give them the kind of nudges that it's much more difficult to do on a sort of open banking basis. So we think that's the way to address this. Clearly, we are also assuming that deposit margin pressure does not ease. So that was back to the question from Ed. So we're not assuming that we find out of this by the end of the year and that there's any difference in the margin pressure in this business. You then need to think about what happens sort of if rates continue to go lower, then you make less and less money out of deposits anyway and you start to make more and more out of assets. That's why it's really important for NII longevity, that there is some diversification within NII. We're very, very focused as an industry, I guess, as a sort of investor group at the moment on the margins within deposits. But we have to grow NII from assets now because the rate cycle will tell you that in low rates, you make more in assets, less in deposits. That will come. And so for those challengers, that is quite a challenge to the model. You can't just be a deposit taker. What do you do with those deposits? How are you going to lend them. So, we do think about it through the cycle, we do think about it on a more holistic basis and technology is really, really important, not only engaging the customer on the deposit side, but also ensuring that we are lending to them and deepening that relationship. In terms of wealth and AI, it depends on what you mean about wealth. So, there's a huge continuum here around how people think about their wealth and how they place it. So, if you go from our Private Banking business, -it's very high touch, very human-led. If you remember that slide that Venkat had, it was the one that's over on the left-hand side, and we would probably see that persisting. So, if you're looking at a Private Banking model, it's going to be predominantly human-led. If you're at the other end where you are an execution-only model like Smart Investor, now renamed Direct Investing, I think, that has to be execution only, completely digital, etc. Then wealth is somewhere in the middle. So, you are going to want to have your customers dealing with you digitally, getting digital prompts. And that's why that advice guidance boundary piece of work that the government is doing is so important because at the moment, the boundary to receiving advice is quite a high one. I give you advice, you pay me. That's what RDR requires. But actually, in advice guidance, it becomes a bit more like people like Rob, looks at things like this. So it's much more prompting guiding. In that kind of environment, you would expect AI to be much more relevant, the kind of nudges and understanding that you have of our customers. That's why we think this link between our 'Premier' and our 'Affluent' customers and that digital link from the app back to the point I made about you get in the app and you stay in that ecosystem and extending that all the way over into wealth, we think is really important. That does not exist in the UK at this point in time. That doesn't exist. So, you can come at it in a couple of ways. You can either buy a predominantly adviser-led wealth business and sort of try and push it right to left or you can go the other way. And obviously, that's what we're trying to do.
